newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists show little sign of compromise.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists show little sign of compromise.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists showed little sign of compromise on Tuesday, saying they would hold talks with the opposition on elections but would propose forming a new government with a programme for 500 days.
The opposition said it still wanted parliament to pass its declaration which sparked a violent siege of the legislature on Friday, and insisted a general election must be held.

The Socialists' parliamentary group approved Monday's leadership statement saying they accepted "in principle" the idea of an early election, but insisted that President Zhelyu Zhelev should give them a mandate to form a new government, in line with the constitution.

Zhelev has declined to invite the Socialists' prime minister-designate Nikolai Dobrev to form a new cabinet to replace the Socialist government of Zhan Videnov, who resigned as prime minister on December 21.
Asked how long the new government should remain in office, Mariela Miteva, a member of the Socialist leadership, said:
"The question is not the term, but the situation. The situation requires that emergency laws for economic stabilisation should be approved, otherwise the country faces economic collapse."
She told reporters that elections should be held "in conditions of civil peace".

The opposition walked out of parliament on Friday after the Socialists refused to vote on their "salvation declaration" calling for early elections and negotations with the Ineternational Monetary Fund and World Bank on an economic programme to be conducted by an all-party team. At least 196 people were hurt in clashes between protesters and police.
"We will negotiate for a new cabinet with a programme for 500 days with as broad a base as possible," she said.
Miteva said the Socialists would attend Sunday's parliamentary session at which opposition president-elect Petar Stoyanov will be sworn in.
Stoyanov said he had agreed to meet Socialist leaders, probably on Wednesday.
Leaders of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) met on Tuesday to discuss the Socialists' offer of talks.
"We approved a decision that the parliament should vote on the "declaration for national salvation"," said opposition deputy and former parliament speaker Alexander Jordanov.
He said the opposition coalition opposed the formation of a new long-term cabinet from the present parliamentary majority.
The quick formation of a new cabinet is seen as vital to secure a new funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund and avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.

At least 6,000 students, three times as many as protested on Monday, marched the five km (three miles) from the student housing district to the city centre carrying blue UDF flags, Bulgarian national flags and one black banner reading "They buried Bulgaria".
They chanted "elections in May", "send them all to Siberia" and "we want a normal life".
Organising elections would take at least three months.
People along the route applauded them and one group held up a banner saying "we are proud of you". Six police cars followed the march.
"We will be in the streets every day until they give up power and admit their guilt over the awful economic crisis in this country," said Sofia University student Violeta Ivanova.
Videnov's government, elected in December 1994, is half-way through its mandate.
The UDF planned a rally in Sofia later on Tuesday and trades union leaders met to discuss sympathy strikes expected to begin on Wednesday.
In the port city of Varna on Monday, dockers staged a short symbolic strike intended as a foretaste of a general strike.

Annual inflation for 1996 was 310.8 percent. The Socialists' critics blame the party's powerful business allies for capital flight which has helped push the lev down to nearly 700 to the dollar from 70 a year ago.
